analysis.one_liner: Bans drugmakers from switching patients to a tweaked drug to block cheaper generics.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: with no cosponsors, it died in the House Judiciary Committee after being sent to a subcommittee, and the Congress ended without any action.
analysis.plain_summary: Brand-name drug companies sometimes 'product hop': as a cheaper generic is about to arrive, they pull the old drug off the market and sell a slightly tweaked version, resetting their patent protection and keeping prices high. This bill would make that a rule violation under the Federal Trade Commission Act, letting the FTC penalize manufacturers, force them to pay back extra profits, and sue in court. It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its antitrust subcommittee, where it sat until the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who take brand-name drugs facing a generic competitor, and the families and insurers paying for those prescriptions. If product hopping were barred, cheaper generic or biosimilar versions could reach the market on the normal schedule instead of being pushed back, cutting out-of-pocket costs. Generic and biosimilar drug makers would also gain access to markets that tweaks currently wall off.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would make a 'hard switch'—pulling a drug from FDA's approved list or announcing its withdrawal, then selling a modified follow-on version—a violation of the FTC Act when it happens as a generic application is pending [S2] [S3].

It would also treat a 'soft switch'—any other action that unfairly disadvantages the old drug relative to the new one and impedes generic competition—as a violation, with the manufacturer allowed to rebut the presumption by showing it was not meant to limit competition [S2].

The FTC could investigate, impose penalties, seek court injunctions, and ask courts to order disgorgement of unjust enrichment and restitution, giving the agency real remedies beyond existing antitrust law [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose profits depend partly on extending exclusive sales periods by reformulating drugs rather than competing on price. Patients could also face small delays for reformulations that would have been legitimate, since the bill requires manufacturers to prove their reasons in each contested case.

drawbacks.text: The bill is written with a presumption and rebuttal process, so a manufacturer that genuinely reformulates for patient safety must prove to the FTC or a court that it would have acted anyway and that safety drove the change, adding legal costs and uncertainty for legitimate innovation [S3].

The prohibition applies only during the window from when a generic application is filed until 180 days after the generic launches, so manufacturers could still time patent strategies around that window [S3].
It relies entirely on FTC enforcement, which is slower and narrower than private lawsuits, so the practical deterrence would depend on the FTC's priorities and resources.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a narrow but real tactic that keeps drug prices high for years at a time, and it includes safety and pro-competitive carve-outs so legitimate reformulations are not banned outright. The cost falls almost entirely on the brand-name industry, with some risk that the compliance burden and presumption discourage good-faith reformulations. On balance, a well-targeted consumer-protection measure that never advanced far enough to be tested or refined.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, then to its antitrust subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. David Cicilline introduced the bill on September 19, 2019, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1] [S5].

On October 2, 2019, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law, and no further action was recorded before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off, since the tactic the bill would have penalized remains unrestricted. The House Judiciary Committee also avoided taking up a measure none of its other members had endorsed.

for.name: David Cicilline
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar drug product hopping as an unfair method of competition under the FTC Act.

against.name: Jerrold Nadler
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill out of committee or scheduled it for a markup or floor vote during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No cosponsors of either party joined the Democratic sponsor, and no vote was ever held, so the bill never showed a clear partisan shape in the record [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill would penalize product hopping—the practice of withdrawing a drug and selling a tweaked version just before a generic arrives—which is a way to extend high-price exclusivity. Its loss would be patients' savings on prescriptions.

The bill would clear the way for generic and biosimilar versions of drugs that product hopping keeps off the market, expanding the segment's market access. Lower competition barriers are also the direct source of savings for patients.
